name: Brad Frost
philosophy: We are not designing pages — we are designing systems of components. Atomic Design provides a shared mental model: atoms (irreducible HTML elements and base tokens), molecules (simple groupings like a search form), organisms (complex sections like a site header), templates (page-level layout structures), and pages (specific instances with real content). The labels matter less than the shared language they create across disciplines. Design tokens are the subatomic layer below atoms — raw, named values (color-brand-primary: #0055CC, spacing-400: 16px) that become every component's DNA when applied. Tokens exist in tiers: primitive (color-blue-600), semantic (color-action-default), and component-specific (button-background-hover). This tiered architecture lets a single change cascade predictably across an entire product ecosystem. The design system is always a means to an end — great, consistent, accessible products serving real people. Design systems are less about assets and more about people and their relationships: shared vocabulary, agreed conventions, trust between designers and developers. Make the right thing the easy thing.
principles: We are not designing pages, we are designing systems of components — the page is a specific instance of a template, not the primary deliverable
Design tokens are subatomic particles: raw, named values (color, spacing, radius, motion) that become meaningful only when applied to components through semantic and component-specific tiers
Atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, pages — the specific labels matter less than the shared hierarchy; adapt the vocabulary to your team's culture and needs

Components exist at three tiers: design system components (content-agnostic, maximally reusable), recipes (product-specific compositions of design system components), and snowflakes (acknowledged one-off components for genuinely unique use cases)

CSS architecture should be explicit and scannable: .c- prefix for components, .l- for layout primitives, .u- for utilities, .is-/.has- for state classes, .js- for JavaScript-only hooks — clarity always trumps succinctness
The Inception Rule: never nest Sass or CSS more than three layers deep — keep selectors flat, DOM-independent, and modular to prevent specificity wars and coupling to markup structure

The web is inherently fluid — embrace responsive design by default, not as an afterthought; container queries complete the vision by enabling true component-level responsiveness independent of viewport
Design and development must work together continuously in a hot loop, not in sequential handoff phases — the phrase should be 'deciding in the browser' rather than 'designing in the browser'
A design system is a product, not a side project — it requires a dedicated product owner, a roadmap, a backlog, regular releases, versioning, adoption metrics, and continuous improvement

Interface inventories are the most powerful persuasion tool for design system adoption: collecting every unique button, card, modal, and form field from a live product and displaying them side-by-side makes inconsistency viscerally, undeniably visible to any stakeholder
signature_quotes: We're not designing pages, we're designing systems of components.
In the world of UI, design tokens are subatomic particles.
Atomic design is not a linear process, but rather a mental model to help us think of our user interfaces as both a cohesive whole and a collection of parts at the same time.
A design system is a means to an end. The end is the thing your users interact with.
Design systems are less about assets and their relationships to one another, and more about people and their relationships to one another.
Let's change the phrase 'designing in the browser' to 'deciding in the browser.'
Clarity trumps succinctness — a verbose, readable class name is always better than a cryptic abbreviation that saves a few characters.
Default to thinking about everything as a design system component — ask how you can design, structure, name, and build it to be as reusable and agnostic as possible.
Make the right thing the easy thing.
One of the most powerful benefits of interface inventories is that you can show them to anyone, including non-designers and developers, and they'll understand why inconsistent UIs are problematic.
A design system in a vacuum is a collection of components. A design system in practice is a set of shared agreements between the people who build products.

championed_typefaces: Source Sans Pro / Source Code Pro (Adobe open-source family for documentation)
Variable fonts broadly (continuous weight/width axes for responsive typography)
typographic_specifics.preferred_weights: Tokenized weight scale rather than specific preferences. Weights defined as design tokens (font-weight-regular: 400, font-weight-medium: 500, font-weight-bold: 700) and applied through semantic aliases (font-weight-heading, font-weight-body). Variable fonts preferred for continuous weight adjustment. No decorative ultra-light or ultra-heavy weights — functional range from 400-700 for most UI work.
typographic_specifics.grid_system: Component-driven layout primitives rather than traditional page-level grids. Composable patterns: Stack (vertical rhythm via gap), Cluster (horizontal wrapping), Sidebar (content + aside), Switcher (responsive column-to-stack), Cover (vertically centered hero), Grid (auto-fill responsive). CSS Grid with fr units and auto-fill/auto-fit for fluid responsiveness. Container queries as the completion of component-level responsive design. No fixed-width page grids — every layout adapts to its container context.

color_palette.rationale: Colors are design tokens, not fixed values. The palette exists as a three-tier token architecture: primitive tokens (color-blue-600: #0055CC), semantic tokens (color-interactive-primary), and component tokens (button-background-default). Brand color changes cascade from one primitive value update. All color combinations must meet WCAG AA contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components). Dark mode is an alternate semantic-to-primitive mapping, not a separate system.

aesthetic.colors: Colors are design tokens in a tiered architecture: primitive (color-blue-600: #0055CC), semantic (color-interactive-primary), component (button-background-default). This three-tier structure lets brand color changes cascade predictably from one primitive through every application. WCAG AA contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) are non-negotiable constraints built into the token layer, not QA polish. Dark mode is an alternate semantic-to-primitive mapping, not a separate system. No hue preference exists; the system and its governance are the aesthetic.
aesthetic.typography: Type scales from modular ratios — Major Third (1.25) for compact UIs, Perfect Fourth (1.333) for editorial — with every value tokenized: font-size-100 through font-size-900. Line heights tied to scale: tight (1.1-1.2) for headings, comfortable (1.4-1.6) for body, generous (1.6-1.8) for long-form. Fluid type via clamp() — e.g., clamp(1rem, 0.5rem + 1.5vw, 1.25rem). Complete font stacks: primary web font, metrically compatible fallback, generic system-font-stack. Variable fonts preferred for performance and continuous weight/width/optical-size axes.
aesthetic.layout: Component-driven layouts from composable primitives: Stack (vertical rhythm), Cluster (horizontal wrapping), Sidebar (content + aside), Switcher (responsive column-to-stack), Cover (centered hero), Grid (auto-fill responsive). Fluid grids using CSS Grid fr units and auto-fill/auto-fit, flexible images with max-width: 100%, media queries as progressive enhancements. Container queries complete component-driven responsive design — a Card reflowing based on container width, not viewport. A single 1440px Figma mockup as sole deliverable is a failure mode. Every component demonstrated at multiple container sizes.
aesthetic.detail: Design tokens as single source of truth: spacing scale on 4px base (space-100: 4px through space-1200: 48px), border-radius scale (radius-sm: 2px, radius-md: 4px, radius-lg: 8px, radius-full: 9999px), shadow/elevation scale, z-index scale, and motion tokens (duration-fast: 100ms, duration-normal: 200ms, easing-default: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)). Every component has fully specified states: default, hover, focus (visible focus ring meeting WCAG 2.2 — never outline: none), active, disabled (aria-disabled preferred), loading, empty, error, success. Documentation includes usage guidelines, accessibility requirements, keyboard patterns, and live code examples.

critique_style: Frost would deconstruct the design into its component hierarchy: 'This Card — is it the same organism as the one on the listing page? Show me the token audit — is this #0055CC from color-interactive-primary or hard-coded?' He catches inconsistencies page-level reviews miss: a 6px radius here, 4px there; a heading one type-scale step off; focus states using box-shadow on one component and outline on another. He walks through states systematically: 'Show me validation error. Loading skeleton. At 320px. Now at 768px in a sidebar — container queries or viewport?' He asks about naming: 'Is the Figma name, the code name, and the docs name all the same?' Collaborative but relentlessly systematic: 'Looks great as a Dribbble shot. Now show me the system underneath it.'
would_approve: Design token architectures with clear three-tier naming: primitive tokens (color-blue-600), semantic tokens (color-interactive-primary), and component tokens (button-background-hover)
Component libraries organized by the three-tier model: agnostic design system components, product-specific recipes, and acknowledged one-off snowflakes with migration plans
CSS files with explicit class prefixes (.c-, .l-, .u-, .is-, .js-) and BEM naming that any developer can read without tribal knowledge
Responsive designs demonstrated at multiple viewport widths simultaneously — never just a 1440px desktop mockup as the sole deliverable
Container queries used for component-level responsiveness so components adapt to their container, not the viewport
Interface inventories used as a persuasion tool for organizational buy-in by making inconsistency viscerally, undeniably visible
Web Components or framework-agnostic component implementations as the interoperable foundation of a design system
Variable fonts specified for both performance (single file) and typographic expressiveness (continuous weight/width axes)
Component documentation that shows all interactive states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, empty, error, success) with accessible focus indicators
Flat CSS architectures with maximum three levels of nesting and no deeply chained selectors coupled to DOM structure
would_reject: Single-screen Figma mockups delivered as the complete design specification with no responsive considerations, no component breakdown, and no token documentation
Design token naming that is purely visual (blue-700 as the only name) with no semantic alias layer (color-action-default) to carry intent
CSS written as a single monolithic stylesheet with deeply nested selectors tightly coupled to markup structure
Fixed-width layouts hardcoded to 1440px that collapse or overflow at any other viewport size
Identical-looking components on different pages that are actually independently coded duplicates rather than shared design system components
Style guides delivered as static PDFs or Figma-only files with no live component playground, no code examples, and no state documentation
Sass nesting deeper than three levels, creating compiled selectors with specificity so high they require !important overrides
Designs where accessibility is treated as a QA checkbox after visual design is frozen, rather than a constraint built into tokens and components from the start
Component names that describe visual appearance ('big-blue-button') rather than purpose or hierarchy ('c-button--primary')
Waterfall handoff workflows where designers complete mockups in isolation and developers re-implement without continuous collaboration
modern_web_take: Frost is actively shaping web design's trajectory. His current work centers on design tokens as cross-platform interoperability — connective tissue between Figma variables, CSS custom properties, and native platform semantic colors. CSS container queries are the missing piece for truly component-driven responsive design — a Card reflowing by container width fulfills the atomic design promise. Web Components are the correct long-term bet for framework-agnostic design system implementations surviving React-to-Vue-to-Svelte migrations. His sharpest critique is organizational: tools are mature enough, but most organizations treat design systems as side projects staffed by volunteers and starved of resources. A design system is a product needing a product owner, roadmap, dedicated engineering, versioned releases, and adoption metrics. His subatomic framing completes the Atomic Design hierarchy with design tokens bridging design intent and code implementation.

Nicole Sullivan (Object-Oriented CSS — the modularity mindset that prefigured component-driven architecture)
Christopher Alexander (A Pattern Language — the conceptual lineage from architecture to software to UI pattern libraries)
BEM (Block Element Modifier naming methodology — the naming convention that made CSS class intent visible)
SMACSS and OOCSS (early modular CSS architectures that introduced categorization to stylesheets)
Pattern Lab (the open-source tool he co-created with Dave Olsen that operationalized atomic design as a build process)
Chemistry metaphor (atoms, molecules, organisms — chosen because it provides a hierarchy that non-technical stakeholders immediately understand)
Progressive enhancement (building from the most basic functional layer upward — the philosophical foundation of resilient web design)
Josh Clark (Big Medium co-founder, responsive design collaborator, and design system consulting partner)
Jina Anne (design tokens pioneer who helped formalize token naming conventions and community standards)
Nathan Curtis (EightShapes — systematic approach to design system component documentation and governance)
